context_edits.new: static final Map<FastDateFormat, FastDateFormat> cInstanceCache = new HashMap<FastDateFormat, FastDateFormat>(7);
context_edits.old: private static final Map<FastDateFormat, FastDateFormat> cInstanceCache = new HashMap<FastDateFormat, FastDateFormat>(7);

ownership_reason: Only the gold creates a formatter: it alone (DateUtils, in FastDateFormat's package) can call the protected constructor and the protected init() and see the class's instance cache, and on a miss it returns and registers the formatter it made. Hops 1-4 (packages text, lang3 and builder, no subclass of FastDateFormat) only pass the pattern, time zone and locale down and the formatter up; none of them can initialise it, and a serialisation round trip (which runs readObject and so init) yields a new instance on every call, which test_getInstance_String_TimeZone rejects (assertSame). The convention is pinned outside the gold: the three-argument FastDateFormat.getInstance initialises every formatter it creates before caching and returning it ('convert shell format into usable one'); FastDateFormat.readObject re-initialises every deserialised formatter (testLang303 formats with one); init is documented as 'Initializes the instance for first use'; DateFormatUtils.format formats directly with the formatter getInstance returns (testSMTP), as testLowYearPadding does with the (String) overload. The gold's javadoc promises a date/time formatter for the pattern; the variant returns one that cannot format (NullPointerException in applyRules). Edits above the gold that call the intact three-argument overload (instead of the next hop, or before it so the gold always hits the cache) pass the suite but replace the gold's formatter with the sibling's: bypasses, not repairs of the chain. A lazy initialisation inside FastDateFormat.applyRules (if (mRules == null) init();) also passes the suite, but it is not consistent with the class: FastDateFormat is documented as thread-safe for multi-threaded use and its formatters are shared through the instance cache, so rules built on first use would be written into a shared instance without any lock (the format methods run unsynchronised and mRules is neither final nor volatile); the class's convention, pinned by the three-argument getInstance ('convert shell format into usable one') and readObject, is that whoever creates or restores a formatter initialises it before handing it out, and the format methods read mRules unguarded because of it.
